intro: This guide explains the sounds of English using the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA). The symbols mainly follow a British Received Pronunciation (RP) model, with notes on common General American (GA) differences.

vowels.description: A long close front vowel. Keep the tongue high and the lips spread.
A short near-close front vowel. It is shorter and more relaxed than /iː/.
A short mid front vowel. In many GA accents this is close to /ɛ/.
A short open front vowel. The mouth is more open than for /e/.
A long open back vowel. In RP it is usually longer than GA /ɑ/.
A short open back rounded vowel common in RP. Many GA speakers use /ɑ/ here.

vowels.spelling: or, aw, au, ore, oor, al
vowels.description: A long mid-back rounded vowel. GA often uses /ɔ/ or /ɔr/ depending on spelling.
A short near-close back rounded vowel. It is shorter than /uː/.
A long close back rounded vowel. The lips are rounded and the tongue is high.
A short mid central-back vowel in stressed syllables, common in RP and GA.
A long mid central vowel in stressed syllables. GA usually has /ɝ/ with r-coloring.

vowels.spelling: a, e, i, o, u, er, or
vowels.description: The schwa, a weak unstressed vowel. It is the most common vowel in English.

diphthongs.description: Moves from a mid front sound toward /ɪ/.
Moves from an open front sound toward /ɪ/.
Moves from a rounded back sound toward /ɪ/.
Moves from an open sound toward /ʊ/.
RP diphthong moving toward /ʊ/. GA often uses /oʊ/.
Moves from /ɪ/ toward /ə/. In GA it is often /ɪr/.
Moves from /e/ toward /ə/. In GA it is often /er/.
Moves from /ʊ/ toward /ə/. Many speakers now replace it with /ɔː/ or /ʊr/.

consonants.description: Made by closing the lips and releasing air without voice.
Made like /p/, but with vocal fold vibration.
Made by touching the tongue to the ridge behind the teeth and releasing air.
Made like /t/, but voiced.
Made at the back of the mouth without voice.
Made like /k/, but voiced.
Made with the top teeth on the lower lip and continuous airflow.
Made like /f/, but voiced.
Made with the tongue near the teeth and no voice.
Made like /θ/, but voiced.
Made with a narrow groove for air between the tongue and ridge behind the teeth.
Made like /s/, but voiced.
A hush sound made with the tongue further back than /s/.
The voiced partner of /ʃ/, common in middle or ending positions.
A breathy sound made at the glottis before a vowel.
A stop followed quickly by a fricative, like /t/ + /ʃ/.
A voiced stop-fricative, like /d/ + /ʒ/.
A voiced nasal sound made with closed lips.
A voiced nasal sound made with the tongue behind the teeth.
A voiced nasal sound made at the back of the mouth.
A voiced sound where air flows around the sides of the tongue.
A voiced approximant. In RP it is often not pronounced before consonants or at word end.
A voiced palatal approximant, like the start of 'yes'.
A voiced labial-velar approximant made with rounded lips.

stress.summary: Stress means making one syllable or word sound stronger. Stressed syllables are usually longer, louder, and clearer.

rules.title: Word stress
rules.text: Many English words have one main stressed syllable. In IPA, primary stress is marked with /ˈ/ before the stressed syllable.

rules.title: Secondary stress
rules.text: Long words can have a weaker second stress, marked with /ˌ/.

rules.title: Noun and verb pairs
rules.text: Some two-syllable words change stress by word class, such as REcord (noun) and reCORD (verb).

rules.title: Sentence stress
rules.text: In sentences, content words usually receive more stress than grammar words.

rules.title: Weak forms
rules.text: Function words like to, for, and can often use weak vowel /ə/ in natural speech.

examples.note: stress moves to the second syllable
noun stress on the first syllable
verb stress on the second syllable

connectedSpeech.title: Linking
connectedSpeech.text: A consonant sound at the end of one word can link to a vowel at the start of the next word.

connectedSpeech.title: Intrusion
connectedSpeech.text: Speakers may insert /r/, /j/, or /w/ between vowels to make speech smoother.

connectedSpeech.title: Assimilation
connectedSpeech.text: A sound can change to become more like a nearby sound.
connectedSpeech.example: good boy → /ɡʊb bɔɪ/ in fast speech

connectedSpeech.title: Elision
connectedSpeech.text: A sound may disappear in fast, natural speech.

connectedSpeech.title: Weak forms
connectedSpeech.text: Unstressed grammar words often reduce to a shorter form.

ukUs.uk: Often not pronounced after vowels unless followed by a vowel.

ukUs.us: Often a flap /ɾ/ between vowels in casual speech.
